title: In What Mirror M. Madeleine Contemplates His Hair
summary: At dawn Jean Valjean, back from Arras, comes to the infirmary where Fantine sleeps; Sister Simplice is shocked to see that his hair has turned white overnight. He insists on seeing Fantine, and when she wakes her first word is a question: "And Cosette?"
details: Day is breaking in Montreuil-sur-Mer. Fantine has had a feverish night full of happy visions and has only just fallen asleep when Sister Simplice, mixing a draught in the dispensary, looks up and finds the mayor standing before her. He has come straight from the courtroom at Arras. The sister tells him Fantine is calmer because she believes he went to Montfermeil to fetch her child, and asks, anxiously, what they will say to her now. "God will inspire us," he answers; the nun murmurs that they cannot tell a lie.

In the full daylight the sister sees that his hair, dark the day before, has gone perfectly white. She finds him the little mirror the doctor uses to test whether a patient still breathes; he looks, says only "Well!" and seems to be thinking of something else. When she suggests he keep away until the child can really be brought, so that no lie is needed, he refuses: he must see Fantine now, because he may be "in haste." The sister does not catch the weight of that word.

He goes in alone. Fantine sleeps, her breathing ragged but her face serene, almost transfigured; the narrator compares her to something about to take flight rather than to die. He stands by the bed as he did two months earlier, looking from her to the crucifix: then her hair was gray and his brown; now hers is gray and his is white. She opens her eyes, sees him, and asks quietly, smiling, where Cosette is.

title: Fantine Happy
summary: Fantine, certain that Cosette has been brought back, chatters joyfully about seeing her, her first communion and the garden they will have, while the doctor and Valjean put her off. Then her face freezes in terror: Javert is standing in the doorway behind him.
details: Fantine shows neither surprise nor doubt; she says she watched him all night in a glory of celestial forms, and asks why Cosette was not laid on her bed for her to find on waking. He cannot answer. The doctor arrives and covers for him: the child is here, but Fantine is still feverish and must be calm before she sees her. Fantine protests, apologizes, promises to be "very good" so that they will bring the child, and asks him about the journey, the Thénardiers, whether Cosette had clean linen and is pretty.

He holds her hand and tells her only that Cosette is beautiful and well, and that she must stop talking so much because it makes her cough. A little girl playing in the yard begins to sing, and Fantine, radiant, is sure it is Cosette's voice; when it fades she turns against the doctor for keeping her child away. Then she drifts into plans: a little garden the mayor has promised, Cosette running after butterflies, learning her letters, and in five years a white veil for her first communion. She laughs.

He has let go of her hand and sits with his eyes on the floor, lost in thought. Her sudden silence makes him look up: Fantine has raised herself in bed, ghastly, her eyes fixed on something at the far end of the room. She cannot speak; she signs to him to look behind him. He turns and sees Javert.

title: Javert Satisfied
summary: Hugo explains how Javert comes to be there: after Champmathieu's acquittal the district-attorney obtained a warrant for Madeleine as the convict Jean Valjean and sent it to Javert, who has brought soldiers to the infirmary. Standing in the doorway, Javert is transfigured by a terrible joy.
details: The narrator goes back a few hours. Valjean left the Arras courtroom after midnight, caught the mail-coach, reached Montreuil-sur-Mer before six, posted a letter to the banker M. Laffitte, and went to Fantine. At Arras, meanwhile, the district-attorney first insisted on convicting Champmathieu anyway; the defence and the presiding judge prevailed and the jury dismissed the case. The prosecutor then turned on Madeleine instead. He conferred with the president (a royalist, offended that the mayor had said "the Emperor" rather than "Bonaparte"), and an arrest warrant was sent by express to Montreuil-sur-Mer for Police Inspector Javert to execute.

Javert, who had returned home straight after giving his evidence, received the order as he was getting out of bed. To a stranger he looked as cool and correct as ever as he climbed the infirmary stairs, but the buckle of his stock sat under his left ear instead of at the nape: for a man who never had a wrinkle in his duty or his uniform, the sign of an inner earthquake. He had requisitioned a corporal and four soldiers, left them in the courtyard, and had the unsuspecting portress point out Fantine's room. He pushed the door open gently and stood in it, hat on, hand in his buttoned coat, his heavy cane hidden behind him, for nearly a minute unnoticed.

When Madeleine's eyes meet his, Javert becomes terrible without moving: the narrator calls it the face of a demon who has found his damned soul. His satisfaction at finally laying hands on Jean Valjean, his pride at having been right all along despite the brief embarrassment over Champmathieu, flood his features. He feels himself the embodiment of justice, order and law, a ferocious archangel, a monstrous Saint Michael with his heel on crime. Hugo insists there is nothing ignoble in him: probity, conviction and duty wrongly aimed remain grand even when hideous, and Javert in his triumph is to be pitied as every ignorant man who triumphs is. It is "the evil of the good."

title: Authority Reasserts Its Rights
summary: Javert seizes Valjean by the collar in front of Fantine, refuses him three days to fetch Cosette, and shouts out that there is no mayor, only the convict Jean Valjean. Fantine, learning that her child was never brought, dies of the shock; Valjean lays out her body, whispers something in her ear, and gives himself up.
details: Fantine thinks Javert has come for her and screams to the mayor to save her. Jean Valjean (the narrator says he will call him by no other name from now on) tells her gently that it is not she Javert wants, then says to the inspector, "I know what you want." Javert's only reply is a roar: "Be quick about it!" He produces no warrant and makes no explanation; for him this arrest is not a beginning but the end of a five-year wrestling match. He strides to the middle of the room and, to Fantine's bewilderment, addresses the mayor as "thou" and grabs him by the collar. Valjean does not resist.

Valjean asks for a private word; Javert refuses to listen to anything not said aloud. In a low voice Valjean begs for three days' grace to go and fetch the dying woman's child, offering to let Javert come with him. Javert laughs: three days to run away, on the pretext of fetching "that creature's child." Fantine hears, and understands that Cosette is not there. She cries out for her daughter and for Monsieur Madeleine. Javert tells her to hold her tongue, rails at a town where convicts are magistrates and prostitutes are nursed like countesses, and declares for all to hear that there is no Madeleine and no mayor, only a thief, a brigand, a convict named Jean Valjean, and that he has him in his grasp.

Fantine rears up in bed, looks from one to the other, tries to speak, and falls back dead, her head striking the headboard. Valjean opens Javert's hand from his collar as he would a baby's and says, "You have murdered that woman." When Javert threatens him with the guard and thumbscrews, Valjean wrenches an iron bar from an old bedstead, walks to Fantine's bed, and tells Javert in a near-whisper not to disturb him now. Javert, trembling, stays by the door rather than call the guard and risk losing him.

Valjean gazes at the dead woman with inexpressible pity, bends and whispers something to her that no one hears; Sister Simplice, the only witness, always said afterwards that she saw a smile come to the dead lips. He arranges Fantine's head on the pillow as a mother would a child's, ties her chemise, smooths her hair under her cap, closes her eyes, kneels and kisses her hand. Then he rises and says to Javert, "Now, I am at your disposal."

title: A Suitable Tomb
summary: Montreuil-sur-Mer turns on its mayor the moment it hears he was a convict. That night Valjean, having broken out of the town jail, slips back into his room, wraps up the Bishop's candlesticks and leaves his money for the poor; when Javert bursts in, Sister Simplice tells her first two lies and saves him. He vanishes toward Paris, and Fantine is buried in a pauper's grave.
details: Javert lodges Valjean in the city prison. Within two hours the town has forgotten everything Madeleine did: he was a galley-slave, his real name some frightful "Béjean, Bojean, Boujean," he will be tried for an old highway robbery, and people who always found him "too good, too perfect" now say they suspected as much. An old lady who reads the royalist Drapeau Blanc calls it a lesson to the Bonapartists. Only three or four people stay loyal, among them the old portress of his house, who that evening, without thinking, hangs his key on its nail and sets out his candlestick as if he were coming home.

Two hours later a hand reaches through her lodge window and takes the key and candle: it is the mayor. He tells her plainly that he broke a bar in a window, dropped from a roof, and is here; she is to fetch Sister Simplice, who is watching over Fantine's body with Sister Perpétue. How he got into the courtyard without opening the gates is never explained. Upstairs he closes his shutters, finds that the portress has tidied his room and laid on the table the two iron tips of his cudgel and the blackened forty-sou piece rescued from the ashes. He writes a label identifying them as the cudgel-tips and the coin stolen from Little Gervais that he mentioned at the Assizes, sets them where they will be seen first, tears up an old shirt and wraps the Bishop's two silver candlesticks in the strips, nibbling a piece of prison bread as he works.

Sister Simplice comes, weeping and trembling; the day has made the nun a woman again. He hands her a note for the curé: everything he leaves behind is to pay for his trial and for the funeral of the woman who died yesterday, and the rest is for the poor. He will not look at Fantine a last time; he is pursued and would only be arrested in her room. Footsteps and the portress's loud protests sound on the stairs, then Javert's voice: there is a light in that room. Valjean blows out the candle and stands in the angle behind the door; the sister kneels at the table. Javert enters, sees the nun and halts, for his veneration of all authority makes a nun a creature who never sins, and he knows Sister Simplice has never lied in her life. He asks whether she is alone; she says yes. He asks whether she has seen the escaped man, Jean Valjean; she says no. He bows and withdraws without even noticing the still-smoking wick. Hugo prays that this lie be counted to her credit in paradise.

An hour later a man in a workman's blouse, carrying a bundle, is walking fast through the trees and mist toward Paris. The curé, judging that a convict and a street-woman deserved no more, keeps as much of the money as he can for the poor and gives Fantine the cheapest possible funeral. She is thrown into the common pit in the free corner of the cemetery, among the first bones that came to hand. Her grave, the narrator says, resembled her bed.

title: What Is Met with on the Way from Nivelles
summary: Hugo opens a long digression: in May 1861 the narrator, walking from Nivelles in Belgium, turns down a path to an old walled farm, learns from a peasant woman that a cannonball hole in its gate dates from a French attack, and that the place is called Hougomont. He is standing on the battlefield of Waterloo.
details: The narrator, "the person who is telling this story," describes a May morning walk in 1861 along the undulating paved road from Nivelles toward La Hulpe, past Lillois and Bois-Seigneur-Isaac, with the reversed-vase church tower of Braine-l'Alleud to the west and a crossroads tavern called At the Four Winds. He reaches a little valley with a stream under the road, an inn with a cart and hop-poles at its door, a girl weeding beneath a yellow poster, ducks on a pond, and a badly paved lane plunging into the bushes.

A hundred paces down the lane he comes to a fifteenth-century wall and a grim Louis XIV stone gateway with two flat medallions, three harrows lying in the flowering meadow before it, a bird singing in a tree. He stoops to examine a large round hollow in the stone at the foot of the gate-pier. A peasant woman comes out and tells him a French cannonball made it, and points out a hole higher up from an iron bullet the size of an egg that did not pierce the wood. He asks the name of the place. "Hougomont." Looking over the hedges, he sees in the distance a mound with something on it like a lion, and realizes he is on the field of Waterloo.

title: Hougomont
summary: The narrator walks through the ruined château-farm of Hougomont, the first obstacle Napoleon met at Waterloo: the courtyard and chapel where men burned and butchered one another, the well filled with three hundred corpses, the orchard where fifteen hundred fell in an hour. Three thousand men died in this one enclosure, so that today a peasant can offer to explain the battle for three francs.
details: Hougomont, once a château and now a farm, was the first knot under Napoleon's axe at Waterloo. The narrator enters the courtyard: a sixteenth-century arch standing amid ruin, an orchard door, a well, chickens, a chapel with a small bell-tower, a growling dog where the English once stood. Here four companies of English guards under Cooke held out seven hours; Napoleon threw his brother Jérôme, the divisions of Foy, Guilleminot and Bachelu, and nearly all of Reille's corps against it and failed. The northern door, which the French broke in and where the brigade commander Bauduin was killed, still hangs patched on the wall; for years bloody handprints marked its posts. Buildings since pulled down made the yard a maze of angles; the French got in and could not hold it, and answered the fire from cellars and garrets by setting the place alight.

In the ruined wing a cracked spiral staircase shows where the English guards cut away the lower steps and fought from above. The chapel saw a massacre: the French held it briefly, were dislodged, and set it on fire; the wooden Christ's feet burned to stumps and then the flames stopped, which the locals call a miracle, while a cannonball carried off the head of the infant Jesus on a fifteenth-century Saint Anne. The walls carry scrawled names from several nations. At the chapel door was found a corpse still gripping an axe: Sublieutenant Legros. Two wells stand in the yard; one has no bucket because it is full of skeletons. The gardener Guillaume van Kylsom, dragged from his hiding place in the cellar and forced to draw water for the thirsty English, was the last to use it; after the battle three hundred bodies were thrown into it, perhaps too hastily, for legend says feeble voices called from it the following night. Van Kylsom's granddaughter, now gray-haired, remembers being carried to the woods at three years old and imitating the cannon.

The orchard beyond is in three parts, garden, orchard and wood, enclosed by walls and a hedge. In the garden, with its ruined balustrade scarred by bullets, six French light-infantrymen trapped among the currant bushes fought two hundred Hanoverians for a quarter of an hour before dying. In the orchard proper fifteen hundred men fell in under an hour: the English had pierced the south wall with thirty-eight loopholes hidden behind a tall hedge, and Soye's brigade, expecting only a hedge, broke against the wall. "Thus Waterloo began." The French took the orchard anyway, climbing with their nails; a Nassau battalion of seven hundred was overwhelmed; Major Blackmann and the German general Duplat died among the apple trees. Every tree still carries its bullet. Hugo totals it: Bauduin killed, Foy wounded, Nassau and Brunswick regiments destroyed, three thousand men cut down, shot or burned in this one hovel, all so that a peasant can now say to a traveller, "Monsieur, give me three francs and I will explain the affair of Waterloo."

title: The Eighteenth of June, 1815
summary: Hugo turns the clock back to 1815 and argues that the rain on the night of 17–18 June lost Napoleon the battle: wet ground delayed his artillery until half-past eleven, giving Blücher time to arrive. He denies that Napoleon's genius had declined, praises his battle plan, and disclaims any intention of writing a military history: he sees a chain of accidents, and judges "like the populace."
details: Exercising "the storyteller's right" to turn back, Hugo returns to June 1815, a little before the events of the first part of his book. Had it not rained in the night, he says, the fate of Europe would have been different: a few drops of water decided the downfall of Napoleon. The battle could not begin until half-past eleven because the ground was too soft for the guns to manoeuvre, and that delay gave Blücher time to come up.

Napoleon was an artillery officer whose whole method was to converge his guns on one point and breach the enemy like a citadel; on the 18th he had 240 guns to Wellington's 159 and counted on them. Had the soil been dry the action would have begun at six and been won by two, three hours before the Prussians could turn the tide. Hugo then poses the question many historians raise, whether Napoleon at forty-six was worn out, reckless, no longer able to scent catastrophe, and answers flatly: "We do not think so." The plan was by universal admission a masterpiece: strike the centre of the allied line, cut it in two, drive the British on Hal and the Prussians on Tongres, take Brussels, throw the Germans into the Rhine and the English into the sea.

He adds that he does not pretend to write a history of the battle; one scene of the story he is telling is connected with it, but the history itself has been written by Napoleon and by a whole constellation of historians. He is a passer-by on the plain, a bystander bending over ground made of human flesh, with neither military practice nor strategic authority; in his view a chain of accidents dominated both commanders, and where destiny is the culprit he judges as the people do.

title: A
summary: Hugo lays the battlefield out as a capital A: the Nivelles and Genappe roads for its legs, the hollow road from Ohain for its crossbar, Mont-Saint-Jean and Wellington at the apex, Hougomont and Napoleon's Belle-Alliance at the feet. The whole battle was the fight for the plateau inside the A; Wellington held the high ground and Napoleon the low.
details: To picture Waterloo, Hugo says, set a capital A on the ground. The left leg is the road to Nivelles, the right the road to Genappe, the crossbar the hollow road running from Braine-l'Alleud to Ohain. The top of the A is Mont-Saint-Jean, where Wellington stood; the bottom left is Hougomont, with Reille and Jérôme Bonaparte; the bottom right is La Belle-Alliance, where Napoleon was. At the centre of the crossbar the final word of the battle was spoken, and there the lion monument now stands. The triangle at the top is the plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean, and the whole battle was the dispute over that plateau; behind it lies the forest of Soignes. The plain is a vast undulating sweep rising toward Mont-Saint-Jean.

Two armies on a field are two wrestlers, Hugo says, each clutching at every bush, wall and fold of ground; a chance hollow can stop a whole army. Both generals had studied the plain; Wellington had looked it over the year before as a possible battlefield. On 18 June Wellington had the good position, above, and Napoleon the bad one, below. Hugo sketches the familiar silhouette of Napoleon on his white horse at Rossomme at daybreak, the small hat, the green coat, the sword of Marengo, and reflects that history's pitiless light now casts shadow where people once saw only rays: the despot's shadow fights the leader's brilliance, and it is a misfortune for a man to leave behind him the night that bears his form.

title: The Quid Obscurum of Battles
summary: The battle opens late, at 11:35, with a French feint on Hougomont and a real assault on the centre at La Haie-Sainte and the English left at Papelotte; both farms fall. From noon to four the fighting dissolves into an obscure melee that no historian can fix, until in mid-afternoon the battle "came to a point."
details: The first phase, Hugo says, is well known: a troubled, uncertain beginning, worse for the English than the French. The night's rain had left guns axle-deep in mud; only the trampled wheat and rye made movement possible. Napoleon, who liked to hold his artillery in hand like a pistol, waited for the sun to dry the ground, but the sun never came, and the English general Colville noted the first cannon shot at thirty-five minutes past eleven.

The French left wing attacked Hougomont with more fury than the Emperor wished; it was partly a feint to draw Wellington leftward, and it failed because the English guards and Perponcher's Belgians held, so Wellington needed to send only a few extra companies. Quiot's brigade struck La Haie-Sainte in the centre and Ney pushed the right wing against Papelotte on the English left, aiming to cut the Brussels road, bar the way to any Prussians and roll Wellington back on Hougomont. Both Papelotte and La Haie-Sainte were taken. Hugo notes the raw English recruits in Kempt's brigade, who fought with a dash that displeased Wellington.

After La Haie-Sainte fell the battle wavered, and from midday to four o'clock there is an obscure interval that Hugo describes as twilight: a fog of colbacks, dolmans, Scottish kilts, Brunswick black and English scarlet, pictures rather than lines. A battle has an incalculable ebb; the two plans deform each other; the line undulates like a thread; what the generals planned is overtaken by what the ground devours. Rembrandt paints such a thing better than a map-maker. No narrator, he says, can fix the shape of "that horrible cloud which is called a battle." Nevertheless, at a certain moment in the afternoon, the battle came to a point.

title: Four O’Clock in the Afternoon
summary: By four o'clock the English are in grave trouble: Picton is dead, La Haie-Sainte has fallen, Ponsonby's dragoons are cut to pieces, and only the heavily reinforced centre on the plateau holds. Wellington, coldly heroic under his elm, pulls his line back behind the crest; Napoleon takes it for the start of a retreat.
details: At four the condition of the English army is serious. The Prince of Orange holds the centre, Hill the right, and Picton, who commanded the left, has been shot through the head at the moment the French lost the flag of the 105th. Hougomont still holds but is burning; La Haie-Sainte has been taken, only forty-two of its German defenders surviving, three thousand men slaughtered in that barn. The Scots Greys no longer exist; Ponsonby's dragoons have been hacked apart by Bro's lancers and Travers's cuirassiers, Ponsonby himself dead of seven lance-thrusts; two divisions are annihilated.

One rallying point remains, the centre on the plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean, backed by the village and a stout sixteenth-century farmhouse off which cannonballs bounce. The English have cut embrasures in the hedges and hidden guns in the brushwood so well that Haxo, sent to reconnoitre in the morning, reported no obstacles; a battalion of the 95th lies hidden in the tall wheat. Behind lies the forest of Soignes, into which no army could retreat without dissolving. Wellington feeds the centre everything he has: Chassé from the right, Wincke from the left, Clinton's division, the Brunswickers, Nassau, Kielmansegg's Hanoverians and Ompteda's Germans, twenty-six battalions in all, a masked battery of sandbags where the Waterloo museum now stands, and Somerset's fourteen hundred dragoon guards behind a rise.

Wellington sits his horse all day beneath an elm near the old mill, impassive while bullets rain and his aide Gordon falls beside him. Asked what his orders are if he is killed, he says, "To do like me"; to Clinton, "Hold this spot to the last man"; to his Peninsular veterans, "Think of old England!" Toward four the English line draws back: the regiments vanish behind the crest into the sunken farm road, leaving only guns and skirmishers visible. "The beginning of retreat!" cries Napoleon.

title: Napoleon in a Good Humor
summary: Napoleon, though ill, is in high spirits all night and morning, joking at breakfast, admiring his deployed army, sure of "ninety chances in a hundred." Hugo then describes how the monument-builders have reshaped the field, and explains the one feature invisible from the French side: the deep hollow road from Ohain cutting across the crest of Mont-Saint-Jean.
details: The Emperor, unwell and uncomfortable on horseback, had never been in better humour. Riding the lines in the storm at one in the morning with Bertrand and seeing the English campfires, he murmured, "We are in accord"; Hugo says fate and he were no longer in accord. He slept not at all, mistook a passing column for Wellington decamping, learned at half-past three that the English were not moving, and at five, told by Belgian deserters that they meant to fight, said, "So much the better." He breakfasted at a kitchen table on a truss of straw with the map spread out, calling it "a pretty checkerboard," joked with Soult and Ney about Wellington's ball in Brussels, and dictated the order of battle. Hugo gathers testimony to his habitual gaiety: the grenadiers whose ears he pinched, the speaking-trumpet joke on the voyage from Elba.

At nine, when the army deployed in five columns with drums and trumpets, he cried twice, "Magnificent!"; by half-past ten it stood in six lines, "the figure of six V's." He pointed out to Haxo the three twelve-pounder batteries that were to open on Mont-Saint-Jean, "four and twenty handsome maids," and, seeing the Scots Greys massing, allowed himself one word of haughty pity: "It is a pity." He took up his second observation post beyond Rossomme and later a third knoll between La Belle-Alliance and La Haie-Sainte, where balls rebounded about him and where he scolded his terrified peasant guide, Lacoste, tied to a hussar's saddle, for trying to hide behind him. The narrator himself has dug rusted shell fragments from that knoll.

Hugo warns that the field is no longer what it was: to raise the huge earthen mound with the lion, the builders carted away the relief of the ground, so that Wellington on revisiting it exclaimed, "They have altered my field of battle!" In 1815 the slope up to the plateau from La Haie-Sainte was steep, made worse by mud, and along the crest ran a feature no distant observer could guess at. The road between the villages of Braine-l'Alleud and Ohain crosses the plateau between the two highways, and in 1815 it was a sunken way, a trench sometimes twelve feet deep with crumbling banks; stone crosses record a Brussels merchant crushed by a cart there in 1637 and a peasant killed by a landslide in 1783. On the day of battle this hollow road, bordering the crest and quite invisible, was, Hugo says, terrible.

title: The Emperor Puts a Question to the Guide Lacoste
summary: Hugo catalogues the morning's setbacks that Napoleon's imperial certainty shrugged off, then shows him at the moment Wellington's line disappears behind the crest: he takes it for a retreat, dispatches a courier to Paris announcing victory, asks his guide Lacoste a question and gets a shake of the head, and orders Milhaud's cuirassiers to take the plateau.
details: On the morning of Waterloo Napoleon was content, and rightly, for his plan was admirable. Hugo then pours out the day's accumulating mischances in one enormous sentence: Hougomont's resistance, Bauduin killed, Foy disabled, Soye's brigade shattered on the hidden wall, guns mired, shells burying themselves harmlessly in mud, Piré's wasted demonstration, Ney's error in massing d'Erlon's four divisions twenty-seven ranks deep to be ploughed by cannonballs, Marcognet's division caught between infantry and cavalry, flags lost, Grouchy's delay, fifteen hundred dead in the orchard of Hougomont and eighteen hundred around La Haie-Sainte. None of it clouded the Emperor's gaze; he never added up the details, only the total, victory, and treated destiny as his equal.

Yet, Hugo observes, a man with the Bérésina, Leipzig and Fontainebleau behind him might have distrusted Waterloo. When Wellington's line drew back, Napoleon half rose in his stirrups with the lightning of victory in his eyes: Wellington cornered against the forest of Soignes would be the conquest of England, Crécy and Agincourt avenged. He swept his glass over the field a last time, studying every bush, the two English barricades on the highways, and the little white chapel of Saint Nicholas at the Braine-l'Alleud crossroads. He bent and asked the guide Lacoste something in a low voice; the guide shook his head, "probably perfidiously."

Napoleon straightened, reflected, and concluded that Wellington had retreated and had only to be crushed. He sent an express galloping to Paris to announce the battle won. Then he found his thunderbolt: he ordered Milhaud's cuirassiers to carry the plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean.

title: The Unexpected
summary: Three thousand five hundred cuirassiers under Ney sweep down into the valley and up the muddy slope toward thirteen waiting English squares. At the crest the leading column discovers the hollow road of Ohain directly under its horses' feet; rank after rank plunges in and is crushed until the ravine is filled with men and horses. Hugo declares that Napoleon could not have won: God had decided his fall.
details: Milhaud's cuirassiers, twenty-six squadrons of giant men on colossal horses with iron breastplates and long sabres, supported by the light cavalry and lancers of the Guard, had been admired by the whole army that morning. The Emperor's order is carried by his aide Bernard; Ney draws his sword and puts himself at their head. In two columns, Wathier's on the right and Delort's on the left, they descend the hill of La Belle-Alliance like a battering ram, vanish into the smoke of the valley, and reappear climbing at a trot through grapeshot up the slope of Mont-Saint-Jean, two immense steel serpents crawling toward the crest. Hugo likens them to the centaurs of Orphic legend storming Olympus.

Behind the crest, unseen and unseeing, the English infantry wait in thirteen squares, two battalions each, in two lines, muskets at the shoulder, listening to the rising thunder of three thousand horses. Then a line of upraised sabres, helmets and gray-moustached heads shouting "Vive l'Empereur!" bursts over the crest like an earthquake. And at that instant, on the English left, the head of the column rears with a frightful clamour: between the cuirassiers and the English yawns a trench two fathoms deep, the hollow road of Ohain. There is no stopping; the second rank pushes the first in, the third pushes the second; horses fall backward crushing their riders; the force meant to crush the English crushes the French, and the ravine yields only when it is filled with living men, over whom the rest ride on. Nearly a third of Dubois's brigade goes into that abyss. "This began the loss of the battle." Local tradition, surely exaggerated, speaks of two thousand horses and fifteen hundred men buried there.

Napoleon had scrutinized the ground before ordering the charge but could not see the road, which made not a wrinkle on the plateau; alerted by the little white chapel, he had probably asked the guide Lacoste about an obstacle, and Lacoste had said no. Hugo says one might almost claim the catastrophe began with that shake of a peasant's head. Could Napoleon have won? No, and not because of Wellington or Blücher, but because of God: a victorious Bonaparte did not fit the law of the nineteenth century; his enormous weight in human destiny upset the balance, and the groans of overfilled cemeteries and weeping mothers had pleaded against him. "He embarrassed God." Waterloo is not a battle but a change of front by the universe.

title: The Plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean
summary: The surviving cuirassiers hurl themselves for two hours on the English squares, which kneel, fire and close up without flinching; seven squares out of thirteen are destroyed, sixty guns taken, six flags captured. The English army is bled white and its staff decimated, yet the centre does not break, and at five o'clock Wellington murmurs, "Blücher, or night!" as bayonets gleam on the heights toward Frischemont.
details: The masked English battery unmasks at the same moment as the ravine: sixty cannon and thirteen squares fire point-blank into the cuirassiers, and General Delort gravely salutes the battery. Decimated but not discouraged, Delort's column, which Ney had deflected leftward as if sensing an ambush, arrives whole and the cuirassiers fall on the squares at full gallop, swords in their teeth, pistols in hand. The English infantry does not stir: the front rank kneels to receive the horses on bayonets, the second shoots them down, the square opens to let a blast of grapeshot through and closes again. The horses leap into the squares and die there; files of men are ground to dust; the squares become craters and the cavalry a tempest. On the far right the 75th Highlanders are almost annihilated, their piper playing Highland airs on a drum until a cuirassier's sabre cuts off his arm and his song together.

Some Hanoverian battalions give way; Wellington thinks of his cavalry, and Hugo notes that if Napoleon at that moment had thought of his infantry he would have won, which he calls the fatal mistake. Somerset's fourteen hundred dragoon guards with Dornberg's Germans and Trip's Belgians fall on the cuirassiers from behind, so that they fight on every side at once; the dragoons are reduced to eight hundred and their colonel killed. Ney comes up with lancers and light horse; the plateau is taken, retaken and taken again; there are a dozen assaults; Ney has four horses killed under him; half the cuirassiers are left on the plateau. Wellington, three-quarters beaten, says under his breath, "Sublime!" Seven squares of thirteen are destroyed, sixty guns taken or spiked, six English flags carried to the Emperor at La Belle-Alliance. One cuirassier and his horse were found dead the next day at the Mont-Saint-Jean crossroads, having pierced the whole English line.

But the centre is not broken; everyone holds the plateau, so no one does, and most of it remains with the English. Both armies are exhausted: Kempt asks for reinforcements and Wellington replies there are none, he must let himself be killed; Ney asks Napoleon for infantry and Napoleon demands whether he is expected to make it. The English are in the worse case. Alten's division is almost destroyed, Uxbridge's knee is shattered, Delancey, Van Meeren and Ompteda are dead, Wellington's whole staff decimated; the Cumberland hussars turn bridle and flee to Brussels spreading panic that reaches Louis XVIII at Ghent, and the roads to Brussels are choked with fugitives and wagons. Wellington has no cavalry left but Vivian's and Vandeleur's brigades. His lips blanch; the Austrian and Spanish commissioners think him lost. At five o'clock he looks at his watch and murmurs, "Blücher, or night!" At about that moment a distant line of bayonets gleams on the heights toward Frischemont.

title: A Bad Guide to Napoleon; A Good Guide to Bülow
summary: The bayonets are Prussian: Bülow's corps, guided by a shepherd through the forest by the one route that could bring artillery out at Plancenoit, arrives after a day lost to mud and a burning bridge. Napoleon had seen the "cloud" at noon and been told it was Grouchy. At five Blücher orders the attack to "give air to the English army," and Prussian cannonballs begin to fall on the Guard.
details: Napoleon's painful surprise is famous: he hoped for Grouchy and got Blücher, death instead of life, Saint Helena instead of the throne of the world. Hugo lays weight on a small shepherd who guided Bülow, Blücher's lieutenant. Had the boy led him out of the forest above Frischemont instead of below Plancenoit, the Prussians would have come up against a ravine impassable for artillery and never arrived; by the Prussian general Muffling's own account an hour's delay would have found Wellington no longer standing.

Bülow had been badly delayed: he bivouacked at Dion-le-Mont, set out at daybreak, bogged his divisions to the hubs in mud, and had to wait at the narrow bridge of Wavre while the French-fired street leading to it burned out, so that his vanguard reached Chapelle-Saint-Lambert only at midday. Had the battle begun two hours earlier it would have been over at four and Blücher would have arrived to find Napoleon victorious. At noon the Emperor himself had spotted the cloud on the horizon and asked Soult what he saw toward Chapelle-Saint-Lambert; Soult levelled his glass and said four or five thousand men, evidently Grouchy. Others on the staff said it was trees. The cloud did not move, and Napoleon sent Domon's light cavalry to reconnoitre.

Bülow's weak vanguard could do nothing alone, and he had orders to concentrate before engaging; but at five o'clock, seeing Wellington's peril, Blücher ordered him to attack, saying, "We must give air to the English army." The divisions of Losthin, Hiller, Hacke and Ryssel deploy before Lobau's corps, Prince William of Prussia's cavalry debouches from the forest of Paris, Plancenoit catches fire, and Prussian cannonballs begin to rain on the ranks of the Guard held in reserve behind Napoleon.

title: The Guard
summary: A third army breaks the battle to pieces: the Prussians come on, the whole English line goes over to the attack, and the Imperial Guard enters the fight at nightfall, shouting "Vive l'Empereur!" in the knowledge that it is going to die. Wellington's guards rise from the hedges and cut it down; Ney, bleeding and magnificent, seeks death and cannot find it.
details: Everyone knows the rest, Hugo says, and tells it in one rush: eighty-six Prussian guns thundering, Pirch and Zieten's cavalry led by Blücher in person, Marcognet swept from the Ohain plateau, Durutte from Papelotte, Lobau caught in flank, the French regiments dismantled, the whole English line resuming the offensive, a gigantic breach torn in the French army, English and Prussian grapeshot aiding each other, and into this collapse the Guard entering the line. Knowing they were about to die, they shouted "Vive l'Empereur!"; history, he says, records nothing more touching than that agony bursting forth in acclamation. As they advanced, at eight o'clock, the clouds parted and let through the sinister glow of a sun they had seen rise at Austerlitz.

Each battalion of the Guard was led by a general: Friant, Michel, Roguet, Harlet, Mallet, Poret de Morvan. When the tall bearskins with their eagle plates appeared in symmetrical lines, the enemy felt a respect for France and those who were winning believed for a moment they were beaten. Then Wellington shouted, "Up, Guards, and aim straight!"; the red English guards rose from behind the hedges and riddled the tricolour with grapeshot, and the final carnage began. In the dark the Guard felt the army dissolving around it and heard the rout behind it, and still advanced, losing men at every step; not a man was missing from that suicide.

Ney, haggard and great with the grandeur of accepted death, offered himself to every blow. His fifth horse was killed under him; sweating, foaming, his uniform torn open, an epaulette half cut away, his eagle plaque dented by a bullet, a broken sword in his hand, he cried, "Come and see how a Marshal of France dies on the field of battle!" He did not die. He asked Drouet d'Erlon whether he was not going to get himself killed, and shouted that he wished all the English bullets would enter his bowels. Hugo adds that he was reserved for French bullets.

title: The Catastrophe
summary: The French army disintegrates at once on every side; Ney tries hatless and swordless to stop the flight and is swept away; Napoleon's last squadrons are spent in vain; the Prussian cavalry slaughters the fugitives all the way to the frontier, Blücher ordering extermination. At nightfall Bertrand and Bernard catch hold of a haggard man turning back alone toward Waterloo: Napoleon.
details: The rout behind the Guard is melancholy. The army yields simultaneously at Hougomont, La Haie-Sainte, Papelotte and Plancenoit; the cry of "Treachery!" is followed by "Save yourselves who can!" A disbanding army is a thaw: everything cracks, floats and falls. Ney borrows a horse and, without hat, cravat or sword, plants himself across the Brussels road to hold back English and French alike, insulting and clinging to the rout; the soldiers flee past him shouting "Long live Marshal Ney!" Napoleon tries to build walls out of what remains of his Guard and spends his last squadrons; he gallops along the line of fugitives haranguing and threatening, and the mouths that shouted for him in the morning hardly recognize him. Caissons are unharnessed so the drivers can escape on the horses; wagons overturn and block the road; men walk over the living and the dead; forty thousand men pour over roads, bridges, fields and woods. "Lions converted into goats."

At Genappe Lobau rallies three hundred men behind a barricade, but one volley of Prussian canister, whose marks can still be seen on a brick gable, scatters them and Lobau is taken. The pursuit is stupendous. Blücher orders extermination; Duhesme, general of the Young Guard, surrenders his sword at an inn door at Genappe to a hussar who takes it and kills him. Hugo, "since we are history," passes sentence: old Blücher disgraced himself. The flight runs through Genappe, Quatre-Bras, Gosselies, Frasnes, Charleroi and Thuin and halts only at the frontier. And who was fleeing in that manner? The Grand Army.

Hugo asks whether this collapse of the bravest army in history was causeless and answers no: the shadow of an enormous right lies across Waterloo, the day of destiny, when something mightier than man made the heroes' brows wrinkle and great souls surrender their swords. Waterloo is the hinge of the nineteenth century; the great man had to disappear for the great century to arrive. "God has passed by." At nightfall, in a meadow near Genappe, Bernard and Bertrand seize by the coat a haggard, gloomy man who has dismounted and, bridle over his arm, is walking back alone toward Waterloo: Napoleon, the sleepwalker of a shattered dream, trying once more to advance.

title: The Last Square
summary: A few squares of the Guard stand like rocks in the stream of the rout and die alone, one by one. At nine in the evening the last, under an obscure officer named Cambronne, is reduced to a handful at the foot of Mont-Saint-Jean; an English general calls on the brave Frenchmen to surrender, and Cambronne answers with a single obscene word.
details: Several squares of the Guard hold their ground amid the defeat as rocks do in running water, waiting for night and death together. Cut off from an army that no longer exists, each regiment dies alone, some on the heights of Rossomme, some on the plain of Mont-Saint-Jean; with them, Hugo says, died Ulm, Wagram, Jena and Friedland.

At twilight, toward nine, one square remains in the fatal valley at the foot of the slope the cuirassiers climbed, surrounded by the victorious English, under a frightful density of fire. It is commanded by an obscure officer named Cambronne. At each discharge the square shrinks and answers, drawing in its four walls; distant fugitives pause to listen to that ever-diminishing thunder. When the legion is a handful, the flag a rag, the muskets clubs for want of cartridges, and the heap of corpses larger than the group of survivors, a sort of sacred terror falls on the conquerors and the English guns go silent. In the dusk the dying men see the ring of lit matches like tigers' eyes and hear the pieces being loaded, and an English general, Colville or Maitland, shouts, "Surrender, brave Frenchmen!" Cambronne replies: "Merde!"

title: Cambronne
summary: Hugo defends repeating Cambronne's word and calls it perhaps the finest thing a Frenchman ever said: the true victor of Waterloo was not Napoleon, Wellington or Blücher but this unknown soldier who answered catastrophe with scorn. The English batteries fire, and when the smoke clears the Guard is dead.
details: If a French reader's susceptibilities forbid repeating the word, Hugo says, he will violate the prohibition at his own risk, for it would mean leaving something sublime out of history. Among those giants there was one Titan, Cambronne. To make that reply and then perish is the grandest thing possible, and it was not his fault that he survived being shot. The winner of Waterloo was not Napoleon, put to flight, nor Wellington, giving way at four and despairing at five, nor Blücher, who did no fighting: it was Cambronne. To thunder such an answer at the lightning that kills you is to conquer.

Hugo piles up what the word does: it answers the rainstorm, the wall of Hougomont, the sunken road, Grouchy's delay and Blücher's arrival; it drowns the European coalition in two syllables; it ends Waterloo with carnival and Leonidas with Rabelais; it loses the field and keeps history. Faced with a victory in which no one is truly victorious, this earthworm of war, offered the mockery of life, finds in his soul the lowest word and makes it the loftiest. He invents the word for Waterloo as Rouget de Lisle invented the Marseillaise, and he hurls it not only at Europe in the name of the Empire but at the past in the name of the Revolution; Danton seems to speak, Kléber to bellow.

At Cambronne's word the English voice answers, "Fire!" The batteries flame, the hill trembles, a last gush of grapeshot rolls out in white smoke under the rising moon, and when it clears nothing is left: the Guard is dead, the four walls of the living redoubt lie prone, with scarcely a quiver among the bodies. So the French legions expired on Mont-Saint-Jean, on the spot where today, Hugo notes, Joseph the postman from Nivelles passes at four in the morning, whistling and cheerfully whipping up his horse.

title: Quot Libras in Duce?
summary: Hugo weighs the commanders: Waterloo is an enigma to winners and losers alike, decided by chance, "the winning number in the lottery." He sets Napoleon's genius against Wellington's calculation, calls it a first-rate battle won by a second-rate captain, and gives all the glory to the English soldier rather than the Iron Duke; it was, he says, more massacre than battle.
details: Waterloo, Hugo says, is as obscure to those who won it as to those who lost; Napoleon saw panic, Blücher fire, Wellington nothing at all, and the historians, Jomini, Muffling and even the admirable Charras, fumble in its dazzle. In an event stamped with superhuman necessity the part of men amounts to nothing. Taking Waterloo from Wellington and Blücher deprives England and Germany of nothing: in that age Germany had Schiller above Blücher and England Byron above Wellington; civilized peoples are not elevated or abased by a captain's fortune. Often a battle is lost and progress is won. What is Waterloo? Not a victory but the winning number in the lottery, the stake won by Europe and paid by France. It was not worth putting a lion there.

Napoleon and Wellington are not enemies but opposites: on one side precision, foresight, method, war regulated watch in hand; on the other intuition, divination, a flaming glance, faith in a star. Wellington was the Barême of war, Napoleon its Michelangelo, and genius was beaten by calculation; both waited for someone, and the calculator's man, Blücher, came while Grouchy did not. Wellington is classic war taking its revenge for the young Corsican who had humiliated the old school in Italy; the academy's rancour wrote "Waterloo" beneath Lodi, Arcola and Mantua. In his decline Napoleon found Wurmser in front of him again, and to get Wurmser it sufficed to whiten Wellington's hair. "Waterloo is a battle of the first order, won by a captain of the second."

What must be admired is England: not her captain but her army, the Scots Greys, the Horse Guards, the Highlanders playing the pibroch under grapeshot, the raw recruits holding against the veterans of Essling and Rivoli. Wellington, ungratefully, called it a "detestable army." England has made Wellington too great and herself too small; the column should bear the statue of a people, not a man, though Hugo expects England, still cherishing the feudal illusion of heredity and hierarchy, to resent that. He marvels at the cleverness of chance, rain, wall, sunken road, Grouchy deaf, one guide deceiving and another enlightening, and concludes it was more massacre than battle: the narrowest front for so many combatants, seventy-two thousand on each side, fifty-six percent French losses, sixty thousand dead. The field is calm now, but at night, he says, a visionary mist rises and the dreamer sees the whole slaughter fought again by spectres.

title: Is Waterloo to Be Considered Good?
summary: Hugo refuses to join the liberals who do not hate Waterloo. It was a counter-revolutionary victory, Europe's monarchies against France and the Revolution, carrying divine right on its crupper; yet progress cannot be stopped, and the counter-revolution, frightened by Paris, was forced to grant a charter and be liberal in spite of itself.
details: There is a respectable liberal school that does not hate Waterloo; Hugo does not belong to it. To him Waterloo is the stupefied date of liberty, an eagle hatched unexpectedly from such an egg. Viewed from the summit, it is intentionally a counter-revolutionary victory: Europe against France, Petersburg, Berlin and Vienna against Paris, the status quo against the initiative, 14 July 1789 attacked through 20 March 1815, the Brunswicks, Nassaus, Romanovs, Hohenzollerns and Habsburgs in solidarity with the Bourbons. The dream was the final extinction of a people that had been in eruption for twenty-six years.

But because the Empire had been despotic, the restored kingdom was forced by reaction to be liberal, and a constitutional order was Waterloo's unwilling result, to the conquerors' regret. Revolution, being providential, cannot really be conquered: before Waterloo it worked through Bonaparte overturning thrones, after it through Louis XVIII signing a charter. Call revolution Progress, and progress Tomorrow; Tomorrow has no bad tools. It uses Wellington to make an orator of General Foy, who falls at Hougomont and rises again in the tribune; it uses the conqueror from without and the gouty invalid from within. By cutting short the demolition of thrones by the sword, Waterloo only turned the revolutionary work into another channel: the slashers had finished, it was the thinkers' turn.

What triumphed at Waterloo, what smiled behind Wellington, trundled barrows of bones to raise the lion's mound and encouraged Blücher's sabres, was the counter-revolution, which murmured the infamous word "dismemberment"; but arriving in Paris and seeing the crater close at hand, it changed its mind and stammered a charter instead. There is no intentional liberty in Waterloo. The counter-revolution was involuntarily liberal, as Napoleon had been involuntarily revolutionary. On 18 June 1815, "the mounted Robespierre was hurled from his saddle."

title: A Recrudescence of Divine Right
summary: Hugo sketches the Restoration that followed: Louis XVIII back in the Tuileries, the white flag and cockade, the old regime varnished with a charter, Napoleon caged at Saint Helena, the Holy Alliance and the Congress of Vienna. Fallen, Bonaparte looms larger than ever and the kings reign uneasily; and all of it, he says, because a shepherd told a Prussian which way to go.
details: End of the dictatorship; a whole European system crumbles. The Empire sinks into a gloom like the expiring Roman world, and Hugo grants that it was wept for by heroic eyes: it had shed over the earth all the light tyranny can give, a sombre light. Louis XVIII re-enters Paris; the dances of 8 July efface the enthusiasm of 20 March; the white flag flies on the Tuileries; the Corsican becomes the antithesis of the Bearnese. Europe adopts the white cockade; the Imperial Guard gives way to the Maison Rouge; the Arc du Carrousel, ashamed of Marengo and Arcola, hides behind a statue of the Duc d'Angoulême; the pauper's grave of the Madeleine is covered in marble for Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette; a column in the moat of Vincennes recalls the Duc d'Enghien; Pope Pius VII, who crowned Napoleon, blesses his fall; at Schoenbrunn a four-year-old shadow may not be called King of Rome. All because, one summer afternoon, a shepherd said to a Prussian in the forest, "Go this way, and not that!"

This 1815 was a lugubrious April: old poisonous realities under new appearances, a lie wedded to 1789, divine right masked by a charter, prejudices and mental reservations varnished with liberalism, the serpent changing its skin. Napoleon had made man both greater and smaller; the people, that cannon fodder so fond of the cannoneer, looked for him everywhere, and a veteran told that he was dead answered, "You don't know him." The kings filled the void with a Holy Alliance, which the field of Belle-Alliance had named in advance.

Against this reconstructed old Europe a new France is sketched, bearing on its brow the star Liberty, and the young are in love at once with the future and with the past, with Liberty and with Napoleon. Defeat has made him greater; Bonaparte fallen seems loftier than Napoleon erect; England guards him with Hudson Lowe and France watches him with Montchenu; Alexander calls him "my sleeplessness," and the kings reign ill at ease with the rock of Saint Helena on the horizon. While he dies at Longwood, the sixty thousand dead of Waterloo rot quietly and the Congress of Vienna makes the treaties that Europe calls the Restoration. And what, Hugo asks, does any of it matter to the Infinite, before whose eye a grub hopping between grass blades equals the eagle soaring between the towers of Notre-Dame?

title: The Battlefield at Night
summary: Hugo returns to the field after the last shot, where marauders who follow every army strip the dead under the full moon despite Wellington's orders to shoot them. One such prowler, with a sutler's cart waiting nearby, robs a buried cuirassier officer of his ring, cross, watch and purse, and in doing so drags him alive from under the corpses in the hollow road. The officer, believing himself saved, asks the man's name: "Thénardier." His own is Pontmercy.
details: Returning "of necessity" to the battlefield, Hugo notes that the full moon of 18 June aided Blücher's murderous pursuit. The English bivouac in the French camp beyond Rossomme and Wellington goes to the village of Waterloo to write his report to Lord Bathurst; the village, which took no part, carries off all the honour from Mont-Saint-Jean, Hougomont, La Haie-Sainte, Papelotte and Plancenoit. Hugo then turns to one of war's hideous features: the dawn after a battle rises on naked corpses. He will not blame the soldier; every army drags behind it a rearguard of stragglers, half brigands and half lackeys, sham invalids, sutlers in little carts with their wives, marauders who belong to no nation and change sides with the victor. Hoche and Marceau had none; Wellington had few, and ordered anyone caught robbing the dead to be shot, yet that night the dead were robbed all the same.

Toward midnight a man is prowling and climbing toward the hollow road of Ohain, neither soldier nor peasant, a ghoul drawn by the scent of corpses, in a blouse like a greatcoat, with no sack but large pockets, stopping to stoop over something silent on the ground and then fleeing on. Some distance off, hidden behind a hovel at the corner of the Nivelles road, a small sutler's wagon with a wicker hood waits with a starving nag, and in it a sort of woman seated on coffers and bundles; perhaps, Hugo says, there is some connection between the wagon and the prowler. Hougomont and La Haie-Sainte still burn at either end of the English line of fires. The narrator pauses to imagine the death of the cuirassiers in the sunken road, alive and laughing one minute and crushed beneath horses the next; the road is now level with the plain, filled with bodies to the brim, a river of blood running out to the Nivelles highway.

The prowler searches this vast tomb, walking in blood. He stops: a hand projects from under the heap, lit by the moon, with a gold ring on its finger. He crouches, and when he rises the ring is gone. As he stands, the hand closes on the skirt of his coat; an honest man would have been terrified, but he laughs, saying he prefers a ghost to a gendarme. Curious whether the dead man is alive, he digs him out and drags him clear: a cuirassier officer of considerable rank, helmetless, his face a mask of blood from a sabre cut, his limbs apparently unbroken because the dead above him had arched over him. The prowler tears the silver cross of the Legion of Honour from his breastplate, takes his watch from his fob and his purse from his waistcoat. At this stage of his "succour" the officer opens his eyes and whispers thanks.

The officer asks who won; "The English." He tells the man to look in his pockets and take his watch and purse; the prowler pretends to search and says there is nothing there, and the officer says he has been robbed and is sorry, for they should have been his. A patrol approaches and the man makes to go; the officer holds him weakly: "You have saved my life. Who are you?" The prowler says he too belonged to the French army, that he will be shot if caught, and that the officer must get out of the scrape himself. His rank: sergeant. His name: "Thénardier." The officer says he will not forget that name, and gives his own. "My name is Pontmercy."

title: Number 24,601 Becomes Number 9,430
summary: Two newspaper extracts of July 1823 report Jean Valjean's recapture in Paris, his trial at the Var Assizes for the robbery of Petit-Gervais, his death sentence commuted to life in the galleys, and his return to Toulon as number 9,430; a large sum he withdrew from Laffitte's bank is missing. With Madeleine gone, the prosperity of Montreuil-sur-Mer collapses.
details: Jean Valjean has been recaptured. Hugo passes over the details by quoting two newspapers of 25 July 1823. The royalist Drapeau Blanc reports that the man known as M. Madeleine, who had revived the jet-and-black-glass industry of a Pas-de-Calais district and been made mayor, was discovered by the police to be the ban-breaking ex-convict Jean Valjean and has been returned to prison; before his arrest he withdrew more than half a million francs, honestly earned, from M. Laffitte, and no one knows where he has hidden it.

The Journal de Paris adds more: he escaped after his arrest, was retaken three or four days later in Paris as he was boarding one of the little coaches that run to the village of Montfermeil, is believed to have used the interval to withdraw six or seven hundred thousand francs and hide them, and was then tried at the Var Assizes for highway robbery with violence committed eight years earlier on a little Savoyard chimney-sweep. He refused to defend himself; the prosecution proved to its satisfaction that he belonged to a band of robbers in the south; he was condemned to death and refused to appeal; the King commuted the sentence to penal servitude for life, and he was taken at once to Toulon. Some papers presented the commutation as a triumph of the priestly party. In the galleys he was given a new number: 9,430.

Hugo adds, so as not to return to it, that everything Madeleine foresaw during his night of hesitation came true. Montreuil-sur-Mer's prosperity vanished with him: foremen set up as rival manufacturers, workshops closed, methods and products were debased, workers scattered, wages fell, bankruptcy followed, and there was nothing left for the poor. Within four years the cost of collecting taxes in the district had doubled, a fact M. de Villèle pointed out in the Chamber in February 1827.

title: In Which the Reader Will Peruse Two Verses, Which Are of the Devil’s Composition, Possibly
summary: A Montfermeil legend says the devil buries treasure in the forest. Around the time the prosecution supposed Valjean had been prowling near Montfermeil, an ex-convict road-mender called Boulatruelle takes to digging in the woods. Plied with wine by Thénardier and the schoolmaster, he lets slip that he saw a man he knew from the galleys carry a small chest into the thicket and come out with only a pick and shovel; he has searched for the spot in vain.
details: Hugo first tells the local superstition: in the Montfermeil forest one may meet at nightfall a black man with horns, digging a hole. Speak to him and you die within the week; dig up his hole after he leaves and you die within the month; flee and you die within the year. The second course, which at least yields a treasure for a month, is the one most often chosen, and a medieval sorcerer-monk named Tryphon left two lines of bad Latin on what the digger finds: a coin, a stone, a corpse, a phantom, or nothing.

Shortly after the time when the prosecuting attorney believed the escaped convict Jean Valjean had been prowling about Montfermeil, villagers noticed that an old road-mender named Boulatruelle, a former galley-slave under police supervision, employed cheaply on the Gagny–Lagny road and thought too humble and too servile toward gendarmes to be honest, had taken to leaving his work early and going into the forest with a pickaxe, where he was seen in the wildest thickets searching and digging holes. Village gossip concluded the devil had appeared and Boulatruelle was after his hoard. Then his excursions stopped and he went back to stone-breaking.

The schoolmaster and Thénardier, the tavern-keeper, remained curious, suspecting a windfall more solid than the devil's. Thénardier shrugged that no one knows who has been in the galleys or will be, and proposed "the wine test." Boulatruelle drank enormously and said little, but from his scattered words they pieced together a story: one morning at daybreak he found a shovel and pick hidden in the underbrush; that evening, hidden behind a tree, he saw a stranger "whom he, Boulatruelle, knew well" (Thénardier's gloss: a comrade of the galleys) going into the densest part of the wood carrying something square like a small trunk; he dared not follow a man three times as strong as he and armed with a pick; two or three hours later, by moonlight, the man came out carrying only the shovel and pick, and in the morning the tools were gone from their hiding place. Boulatruelle concluded that a chest too small for a body, hence full of money, had been buried, and he had dug wherever the ground looked freshly turned, in vain. Montfermeil forgot the matter, except for a few gossips who were sure the devil had come.

title: The Ankle-Chain Must Have Undergone a Certain Preparatory Manipulation to Be Thus Broken with a Blow from a Hammer
summary: In late October 1823 the battered warship Orion puts into Toulon for repairs. When a sailor is left dangling from a yard, a white-haired life convict breaks his ankle chain with one hammer blow, climbs the rigging and saves him; descending, he falls between two ships and is not found. The Toulon paper reports the drowning of convict number 9,430, Jean Valjean.
details: Toward the end of October 1823 the ship of the line Orion, part of the Mediterranean squadron, enters the port of Toulon after heavy weather. Hugo pauses on the twenty-two useless salute guns and reckons the civilized world fires 150,000 pointless shots a day while the poor starve. He then digresses on "the Spanish war" of 1823: a Bourbon family affair in which France, under the Duc d'Angoulême, marched to crush Spanish liberals, with Napoleon's old soldiers under the white cockade, citadels bought rather than taken, little blood and no honour, a war that wounded the military spirit and enraged the democratic one. The Bourbons mistook it for strength and took the soldier's obedience for the nation's consent; 1830, he says, had its germ in 1823.

He returns to the Orion and to a long hymn to the ship of the line, a floating forest of three thousand cubic metres with a mainmast sixty fathoms tall, a masterpiece of man that a gale can nevertheless snap like straw; this is why crowds gather to stare at warships. The Orion, barnacled and leaking after an earlier scraping had loosened the bolts of her keel, had been further damaged in an equinoctial gale and was anchored near the Arsenal for repairs, watched daily by idlers on the quays.

One morning the crowd sees an accident: a topman bending the main-topsail loses his footing and is left hanging from a footrope, swinging over the sea like a stone in a sling, slowly losing his strength while the newly levied sailors dare not go to him. Suddenly a man in the red jacket and green cap of a life convict climbs into the rigging like a cat; a gust takes his cap and shows a head of perfectly white hair. A convict from the detachment working aboard had asked the officer of the watch for permission to risk his life, and on a nod had broken the chain riveted to his ankle with one blow of a hammer, a thing no one noticed at the time. He runs out along the yard, fastens a rope, lowers himself hand over hand until two men hang over the gulf instead of one, lashes the sailor to the rope, climbs back and drags him up, and carries him along the yard to the top and the arms of his comrades. The crowd applauds, old convict-sergeants weep, and every voice cries, "Pardon for that man!"

Descending to rejoin his detachment he seems to stagger on a lower yard, and a shout goes up: he has fallen into the sea between the Orion and the frigate Algésiras. Four men put off in a boat; the man never surfaces; they sound and dive until evening and do not find even the body. Next day the Toulon newspaper reports, under the date 17 November 1823, that a convict of the Orion detachment, returning from rescuing a sailor, fell into the sea and drowned, his body presumably caught among the piles of the Arsenal point; he was committed under the number 9,430 and his name was Jean Valjean.

title: The Water Question at Montfermeil
summary: Montfermeil in 1823 is a forest village short of water: the church end draws from a spring a quarter of an hour away, and after the water-carrier stops at nightfall whoever needs water fetches it. Cosette, kept as the Thénardiers' servant since her mother stopped paying, dreads being sent to the spring in the dark. On Christmas Eve the tavern is full of carters while she knits under the table.
details: Hugo describes Montfermeil, on the plateau between the Ourcq and the Marne: in 1823 not yet a resort of plaster villas but a cheap, charming forest village on the road to nowhere, whose one hardship was water. The Gagny end used the woodland ponds; the end around the church, where the Thénardier tavern stood, had only a little spring halfway down the slope toward Chelles, a quarter of an hour away. Better houses paid a water-carrier half a farthing a bucket, but he worked only till seven in summer and five in winter, and after dark anyone who wanted water fetched it himself.

This was the terror of little Cosette. The Thénardiers had profited from her twice over, making the mother pay and the child serve, and when the mother's payments stopped they simply kept her as their servant; it was she who ran for water, and she took great care there was always some in the house so that she would never be sent to the spring at night.

Christmas of 1823 is mild and lively: Paris showmen have set up booths in the main street and the Church Square, spreading into Boulanger Alley where the Thénardiers' inn stands, and a menagerie shows a Brazilian vulture with a tricolour cockade for an eye, which retired Bonapartist soldiers come devoutly to see. On Christmas Eve the public room is full of carters and peddlers drinking and smoking by candlelight; Madame Thénardier tends the supper roasting on the fire while her husband drinks with the customers and talks politics about the Spanish war, amid talk of vintages, milling and mowing. Cosette sits in her usual place on the crossbar of the kitchen table, in rags and wooden shoes, knitting woollen stockings for the Thénardier girls; Éponine and Azelma can be heard laughing in the next room; a cat-o'-nine-tails hangs on a nail by the chimney. From somewhere in the house comes the crying of a little boy, three years old, born to the Thénardiers one winter, whom his mother nursed but does not love and leaves to shriek in the dark.

title: Two Complete Portraits
summary: Hugo draws the Thénardiers in full: she is a huge, violent, bearded virago who does all the work and loves no one but her daughters; he is a small, sickly-looking, cunning innkeeper and swindler who poses as a man of letters and tells of saving a wounded general at Waterloo, having in fact followed the armies as a marauding sutler. Between them Cosette is ground like a fly in a spider's web.
details: Thénardier has just turned fifty; his wife is nearing forty, which in a woman, Hugo says, equals fifty. She is tall, blond, red, fat and square, one of those colossal fairground women; she does all the housework, with Cosette as her only servant, a mouse in the service of an elephant. She has a beard, swears splendidly, can crack a nut with her fist and reads sentimental romances; to hear her speak is to think of a gendarme, to see her drink a carter, to see her handle Cosette the hangman.

Thénardier is small, thin, pale and feeble-looking and in fact perfectly healthy; he smiles habitually as a precaution and is almost polite to everyone, even the beggar he refuses. He has the glance of a polecat and the bearing of a man of letters, drops the names of Voltaire, Raynal and Saint Augustine, claims to have "a system," and is a scientific thief. He likes to tell how, as a sergeant at Waterloo, he alone covered with his body and saved a dangerously wounded general under grapeshot, which gave his tavern its sign and its name, the Sergeant of Waterloo. He is a liberal and a Bonapartist and is said to have studied for the priesthood; Hugo thinks he studied in Holland for an innkeeper, some Fleming from Lille at home on both sides of the frontier. As for his Waterloo prowess, the reader already knows what it was and may notice that he exaggerates a trifle: in June 1815 he belonged to the marauding sutlers who follow armies in rickety carts with wife and children, attaching themselves to the winning side, and his little capital of purses, watches, rings and silver crosses gathered from the dead set him up at Montfermeil.

Everyone takes the wife for the master; in truth the frail husband rules the mastodon with a word or a sign, and she adores and fears him. She loves no one but her children, and her maternity, Hugo notes, stops at her daughters and does not extend to boys. He thinks only of getting rich and fails, ruining himself at Montfermeil; in 1823 he owes some fifteen hundred francs in petty debts, which worries him. He is an admirable poacher and a theorist of hospitality, whose creed is to sell the traveller everything, down to the flies his dog eats. Ruse and rage wedded, Hugo calls them, a hideous team.

Cosette is between them, ground in a mill and torn with pincers at once. The woman's method is blows; the man's is that she goes barefoot in winter. She runs up and down stairs, washes, sweeps, scrubs and carries heavy loads, weak as she is, with no mercy from either; the tavern is a spider's web in which she lies trembling. The child says nothing.

title: Men Must Have Wine, and Horses Must Have Water
summary: Cosette, eight years old and black-eyed from a blow, prays silently that no one will need water tonight. A peddler complains that his horse has not been watered; Cosette lies that it has, is caught, and Madame Thénardier sends her out into the pitch-black night with a bucket bigger than she is and a fifteen-sou piece to buy bread on the way back.
details: Four new travellers have arrived. Cosette, though only eight, reflects with the gloomy air of an old woman; her eye is blackened from Madame Thénardier's fist, which the woman uses as a joke about how ugly she is. She thinks that it is very dark, that the pitchers upstairs must have been filled, and that there is no more water in the cistern; she is reassured only because no one in that house drinks water. When Madame Thénardier draws a glass from the cistern and finds only a trickle, the child stops breathing, but the woman decides it is enough.

Then a peddler lodging at the inn comes in and says harshly that his horse has not been watered. Madame Thénardier says it has; he insists it has not. Cosette crawls out from under the table and swears the horse drank a whole bucketful and that she talked to him; it is a lie, and the peddler, who knows how his horse blows when thirsty, calls her a little jade. Madame Thénardier agrees the beast must be watered, hunts out "that other beast" cowering among the drinkers' feet, and orders "Mademoiselle Dog-lack-name" to go and water the horse. Cosette says feebly that there is no water. The woman flings the street door open: then go and get some.

Cosette fetches the empty bucket from the chimney corner; it is bigger than she is and she could have sat in it. Grumbling that there is plenty at the spring and that she should have strained her onions, Madame Thénardier rummages in a drawer and hands "Mam'selle Toad" a fifteen-sou piece to buy a big loaf at the baker's on the way back. Cosette puts the coin in the little pocket of her apron and stands motionless before the open door, as if waiting for someone to rescue her. "Get along with you!" The door closes behind her.

title: Entrance on the Scene of a Doll
summary: Directly opposite the tavern door stands a toy stall whose centrepiece is a magnificent two-foot doll in pink crepe with real hair, too dear for any mother in Montfermeil. Cosette, bucket in hand, stops spellbound before "the lady" and forgets her errand until Madame Thénardier's voice sends her fleeing down the street.
details: The line of booths from the church runs as far as the Thénardiers' inn and is all lit up for the crowds going to midnight mass, an effect the schoolmaster, drinking at the tavern, calls magical; there is not a star in the sky. The last stall, exactly opposite the tavern door, is a toyshop glittering with tinsel, glass and tin, and in front of it, on white napkins, sits an immense doll nearly two feet tall, in a pink crepe dress with gold wheat-ears in her real hair and enamel eyes. All day it has drawn every child under ten, but no mother in Montfermeil is rich or extravagant enough to buy it. Éponine and Azelma have spent hours gazing at it, and even Cosette has stolen a glance.

Coming out with her bucket, Cosette cannot help lifting her eyes to the doll, which she calls "the lady." She has never seen it close. The shop is a palace to her, the doll a vision of joy, splendour and riches; she measures with a child's sad sagacity the abyss between herself and it, decides one must be a queen or at least a princess to own such a thing, and thinks how happy the doll must be. The other dolls behind seem fairies and genii, and the pacing merchant something like God the Father. In this adoration she forgets everything, even her errand, until Madame Thénardier, glancing into the street, shouts at the "silly jade" and "little monster" to get along. Cosette flees, dragging her pail, with the longest strides she can manage.

title: The Little One All Alone
summary: Cosette walks out of the lit village into the black fields and forest, turns back in terror, and then, more afraid of Madame Thénardier than of the dark, runs to the spring. She fills the bucket, unknowingly spilling the fifteen-sou piece into the water, and sits paralysed under a red, setting Jupiter until counting aloud breaks the spell. Staggering back with the bucket, she cries, "O my God!" and a huge hand silently lifts the weight: a man is walking beside her, and she is not afraid.
details: Since the tavern is at the church end of the village, Cosette must go to the spring in the forest toward Chelles. She looks at no other stall; beyond the last lights she plunges into darkness, rattling the bucket handle for company. A woman who sees her mutters about a werewolf child, then recognizes her: "it's the Lark!" Cosette keeps a tolerable boldness while there are walls on either side, but at the last house she stops and scratches her head in a child's gesture of terror and indecision: before her lie the open fields, beasts walking in the grass, spectres in the trees. She turns back, resolving to say there was no water; a hundred paces on she stops again, seeing Madame Thénardier's hyena mouth before her, and it is from the Thénardier that she recoils. She runs out of the village and into the forest, no longer looking or listening.

The spring is only seven or eight minutes from the edge of the wood and she knows the way by day; instinct guides her and she does not get lost. It is a little clay basin about two feet deep, edged with moss and tall grasses, with a brook running from it. Holding a young oak that leans over the water, she bends and plunges the bucket in, so violently excited that her strength is trebled; she does not notice that her apron pocket empties itself into the spring and the fifteen-sou piece sinks. She drags out the bucket nearly full and collapses on the grass, exhausted.

Above her the sky is black cloud; Jupiter is setting through mist, swollen and ruddy like a luminous wound, and the unfamiliar star terrifies her. The forest is dark and wintry, the grasses undulating like eels, nettles twisting like clawed arms. Hugo meditates on the dread of night in a forest, which no stoutness of heart escapes and which is indescribably sinister for a child: forests are apocalypses. Cosette feels seized by the black enormity of nature, something worse than fear; she begins by instinct to count aloud to ten, over and over, and this brings her back to herself. Her wet hands are cold; she has one thought, to flee to the lighted windows; but such is her fear of the Thénardier that she dare not go without the water.

She can barely lift the bucket. She goes a dozen paces and must set it down, then a little further, bent double like an old woman, the iron handle freezing her hands, cold water splashing her bare legs, in the depths of a forest at night in winter, a child of eight seen by no one but God, and, Hugo adds, surely by her mother. She dares not even weep for fear of the Thénardier, whom she always imagines present. At an old chestnut tree she knows she takes a last long rest, lifts the bucket again, and cannot keep from crying, "O my God! my God!"
