At that moment the bucket weighs nothing: an enormous hand has taken the handle. A tall black form is walking beside her, a man who came up behind her unheard and has silently taken her burden. There are instincts for all the encounters of life. The child is not afraid.

title: Which Possibly Proves Boulatruelle’s Intelligence
summary: That same Christmas afternoon a white-haired man in a threadbare yellow coat, poor but scrupulously clean, is seen looking for lodgings on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital in Paris; he shrinks from Louis XVIII's passing carriage, shakes off a police agent, and takes the Lagny coach, leaving it at Chelles after dark. He goes into the Montfermeil forest, checks a particular clearing of stones and marked trees to see that the ground is undisturbed, and then comes upon Cosette with her bucket.
details: On the afternoon of Christmas Day 1823 a man walks the most deserted stretch of the Boulevard de l'Hôpital in the faubourg Saint-Marceau, apparently seeking a lodging, and the narrator says he did in fact hire a room in that isolated quarter. He is the type of the well-bred beggar: extreme poverty and extreme cleanliness, an old well-brushed round hat, a threadbare ochre-yellow coat, black breeches gray at the knee, buckled shoes. His white hair and worn face suggest more than sixty, his vigorous tread barely fifty; there is something severe and humble in the set of his lip and a melancholy serenity in his eyes. In his left hand he carries a small bundle in a handkerchief; in his right he leans on a hedge-cut cudgel dressed up with a red wax head to look like a cane.

At that period Louis XVIII drove nearly every day to Choisy-le-Roi, and his gilded carriage thundered along the boulevard at two o'clock, a clock for the poor women of the quarter; Hugo describes the fat, crafty-eyed, impotent king who could not walk and so loved to gallop, and the local verdict, "That big fellow yonder is the government." The stranger, evidently not of the quarter, is surprised by the cavalcade and hides behind a wall, which does not prevent the Duc de Havré, sitting opposite the king, from remarking an evil-looking man. A police agent is ordered to follow him and loses him in the twilight streets, as a report that evening to the Prefect of Police records.

The man doubles his pace, often looking back, pauses at the Porte Saint-Martin theatre to read a poster for a play called The Two Convicts, and at the Pewter Platter takes the last seat, beside the driver, on the half-past-four coach for Lagny, paying his fare to Lagny after the coachman eyes his shabby clothes. He answers only in monosyllables. At six they reach Chelles, where he gets down with his bundle and cudgel and vanishes without entering the inn; the coachman observes that a man who pays to Lagny and stops at Chelles on a night when every house is shut must have dived through the earth.

He strides down the main street of Chelles, turns right before the church onto the Montfermeil crossroad like someone who knows the country, hides in a ditch when he hears passers-by on the Gagny–Lagny road, then leaves the road and enters the forest. There he slows, examining the trees as if following a secret path, loses his way for a moment, and reaches a clearing with a great heap of whitish stones. He inspects the stones, passes his hand over the warts on the bark of a nearby ash, stands on tiptoe to touch a band of zinc nailed to a peeling chestnut opposite, and treads the ground between tree and stones like a man making sure the soil has not been disturbed. Then he takes his bearings and walks on through the woods toward Montfermeil. It was this man who had just met Cosette: he had seen a tiny shadow groaning under an enormous bucket, setting it down and taking it up, and had come up and silently taken the handle.

title: Cosette Side by Side with the Stranger in the Dark
summary: Walking back to the village with the bucket, the stranger questions Cosette: she is eight, has no mother that she knows of, works all day for Madame Thénardier at the inn while Ponine and Zelma play with their dolls, and has only a little lead sword for a toy. When she says her name he seems to receive an electric shock. He says he will lodge at the inn, and at the door she asks for the bucket back so that she will not be beaten.
details: The man speaks in a grave, almost bass voice: what she carries is very heavy for her. He takes the bucket and walks beside her, muttering that it really is heavy. She is eight; she has come from the spring in the forest; the inn is a good quarter of an hour away. Abruptly he says, "So you have no mother." She does not know; other people have mothers and she has none; she thinks she never had one. He sets down the bucket, puts both hands on her shoulders and tries to see her thin, sickly face in the dark, and asks her name. "Cosette." He seems to receive an electric shock, looks at her again, picks up the bucket and walks on.

She lives at Montfermeil; Madame Thénardier, her mistress, who keeps the inn, sent her for water. In a voice he tries to keep indifferent but which trembles, he asks what Madame Thénardier does, then says he will lodge there tonight and she must show him the way. Cosette follows without fatigue, looking up at him from time to time with a confidence she cannot name; never taught to pray, she feels something like hope rising in her. There is no servant in the house; she is alone there, except for two little girls, Ponine and Zelma, Madame Thénardier's young ladies, who have beautiful dolls full of gold and play all day long. And she? She works, all day long, she says gently, a tear in her great eyes. When they let her she amuses herself as best she can; the girls will not lend her their dolls, and she has only a little lead sword, no longer than her finger, which cuts salad and the heads of flies.

They reach the village, pass the baker's without Cosette remembering the bread, and he falls into gloomy silence. Seeing the booths he asks whether there is a fair; no, it is Christmas. Near the tavern Cosette timidly touches his arm and asks whether she may take her bucket now: if Madame sees that someone carried it for her, she will beat her. He hands it to her, and a moment later they are at the door.

title: The Unpleasantness of Receiving Into One’s House a Poor Man Who May Be a Rich Man
summary: The Thénardiers take the shabby stranger for a beggar and charge him double. He watches Cosette, saves her from the whip over the lost fifteen sous by "finding" a twenty-sou piece, buys the stockings she is knitting for five francs so that she may play, and when she is caught cradling Éponine and Azelma's abandoned doll and weeps, goes out and returns with the splendid doll from the stall, which she names Catherine. He sits up all night; before going to the best room, he finds Cosette asleep under the stairs and puts a gold louis in the wooden shoe she has set on the hearth.
details: Madame Thénardier greets Cosette with abuse, then switches to her innkeeper's smile for the gentleman wanting a lodging, and back to scowling when she sees his threadbare coat and battered hat and her husband signals "a regular beggar." She has no room; he says to put him anywhere and he will pay as for a room; she names forty sous, double the usual price, since she does not lodge poor folks for less. He sits with a bottle of wine he barely touches and watches Cosette, back under the table at her knitting. Hugo describes the child in detail: thin and pale, looking six rather than eight, eyes sunk in shadow and almost put out with weeping, a mouth curved in habitual anguish, hands ruined with chilblains, a rag of linen for clothing and black-and-blue marks where the Thénardier has touched her; her whole body expresses one idea, fear. She has never prayed or set foot in a church.

The Thénardier remembers the bread. Cosette lies that the baker's was shut; the woman demands the fifteen-sou piece back, and Cosette, turning her pocket inside out, finds nothing and is petrified. The woman reaches for the cat-o'-nine-tails; the stranger, who has been fumbling in his fob, bends to the floor, says he saw something roll from the child's apron, and holds out a coin. It is a twenty-sou piece, not fifteen, but the Thénardier pockets it with a glare at Cosette. Éponine and Azelma come in, pretty, plump, warmly and prettily dressed, and settle in the chimney corner with a doll; to them Cosette is a dog. When the Thénardier catches Cosette watching them instead of knitting and threatens the whip, the stranger says timidly, "let her play," and, learning that she is knitting stockings for the daughters worth thirty sous, buys them for five francs, lays the coin on the table and tells Cosette, "Now I own your work; play, my child." Thénardier pockets the coin and tells his wife he has seen millionaires in coats like that. Cosette dresses her little lead sword in rags and sings it to sleep, while the sisters swaddle the cat. Hugo reflects on the doll as the first form of motherhood.

The Thénardier, now calling him Monsieur, sidles up and explains that the child is not theirs but a little beggar taken in from charity, a sort of imbecile with water on the brain, whose mother in her native place has not answered in six months and must be dead; her mother "didn't amount to much" and abandoned her. Cosette, under the table, half hears and rocks her sword-baby singing, "My mother is dead!" The man orders bread and cheese for supper; the woman decides he is a beggar after all. Cosette sees the sisters' discarded doll on the floor, creeps out when no one is watching and takes it back to her corner; only the traveller sees. A quarter of an hour of ecstasy ends when Azelma spots a pink foot in the firelight. Éponine runs to her mother; the Thénardier shrieks "Cosette!" twice; Cosette lays the doll down with veneration and despair, wrings her hands, and, for the first time in the whole terrible day, bursts into sobs. The traveller asks what the matter is; the woman says the beggar has touched the children's doll with her dirty hands. He walks out the street door, and the Thénardier kicks Cosette under the table. He returns carrying the fabulous doll from the stall opposite and stands it in front of her: "Here; this is for you."

Cosette retreats under the table as if from the sun; the whole room falls silent. Thénardier, scenting money, mutters to his wife that the thing cost at least thirty francs and she must grovel; both urge Cosette in honeyed voices to take her doll. She asks permission of Madame, then of the stranger, whose eyes are full of tears, seizes the doll, and announces, "I shall call her Catherine." She sets Catherine on a chair and sits on the floor gazing at her, and when told to play says, "Oh! I am playing." The Thénardier, who hates the man more than anyone in the world at that moment, sends her daughters and then Cosette to bed; Cosette goes with Catherine in her arms. The wife rages in whispers about forty-franc dolls for a jade she would sell for forty sous; the husband answers that a traveller may do as he likes so long as he pays. The other customers now regard the stranger with awe. The mass ends, the inn empties, and the man sits unmoving until two in the morning, when the wife goes to bed, and three, when Thénardier, who has read his newspaper three times, asks whether Monsieur is going to his "repose," a word that swells a bill, and leads him to the mahogany bridal chamber, whose wedding bonnet under glass he lies about, since he bought the whole room second-hand. In their own room his wife says she will turn Cosette out tomorrow; he says only, "How you do go on!"

Alone, the traveller takes off his shoes, takes a candle, and follows the sound of a child breathing to a triangular recess under the staircase, where among old papers and cobwebs Cosette sleeps fully dressed on a holed straw pallet with no sheets, clutching the doll whose open eyes glitter in the dark, one wooden shoe beside her. Through an open door he sees the two little white beds of Éponine and Azelma, and behind them the cradle of the little boy who cried all evening. On the cold hearth he finds two dainty children's shoes, set out on Christmas Eve for the good fairy, each already holding a bright new ten-sou piece from their mother; and in the darkest corner a frightful wooden sabot caked in ashes and mud, which Cosette, with the trust of a child who has never been anything but disappointed, has placed there too. There is nothing in it. He puts a louis d'or in Cosette's shoe and goes back to his room with the stealthy tread of a wolf.

title: Thénardier and His Manouvres
summary: Before dawn Thénardier draws up a bill of twenty-three francs. The stranger pays without a word, asks whether they would like to be rid of Cosette, and the wife joyfully agrees; Thénardier then steps in, protesting that he adores the child, and finally names his price, fifteen hundred francs, which the man lays on the table. Cosette, who found the gold piece in her shoe, is dressed in the mourning clothes from his bundle, and at daybreak the two walk out of Montfermeil on the road toward Livry.
details: Two hours before daybreak Thénardier sits by a candle composing the bill while his wife watches in religious admiration and the Lark sweeps the stairs: supper three francs, room ten, candle five, fire four, service (spelled "servisse") one, total twenty-three francs. She fears it is too much and that he will not pay; Thénardier laughs coldly, says he will pay, reminds himself that he owes fifteen hundred francs, tells her to hand the bill to the man, and goes out. When she again declares she will turn Cosette out today, he only says, "How you do go on!"

The traveller comes down with his bundle and cudgel; Thénardier reappears silently behind him in the half-open door, visible only to his wife. She, unusually embarrassed, hands him the bill; he glances at it absently and asks instead whether business is good. She laments hard times, taxes, and above all the cost of "the little one, the Lark as she is called hereabouts," who has more the air of a bat; she has daughters of her own to raise. In a voice he strives to keep indifferent he asks, "What if one were to rid you of her?" Her face brightens hideously: take her, keep her, carry her away, and the blessings of all the saints on him. Agreed; immediately; call the child. He looks at the bill, repeats "Twenty-three francs?" in a tone between exclamation and question, lays down five five-franc pieces, and tells her to fetch Cosette.

Now Thénardier advances: Monsieur owes twenty-six sous, twenty for the room and six for supper; as for the child, he must discuss that with the gentleman alone. His dazzled wife withdraws. Thénardier, all good-fellowship, declares that he adores the child, has brought her up since she was tiny, has spent four hundred francs on her medicines, cannot give away a child to a passer-by without knowing where she is going, and would need at least some scrap of a passport. The stranger answers gravely that one needs no passport to travel five leagues from Paris; if he takes Cosette he takes her, Thénardier will never know his name or residence or where she is, and she will never see him again. Yes or no? Thénardier, who has watched him all night like a cat and puzzled over who this man can be, grasps that he is dealing with someone very strong whose mystery is simple and unanswerable, and unmasks his batteries: "Sir, I am in need of fifteen hundred francs." The man takes three banknotes from an old black pocketbook, lays his thumb on them, and says, "Go and fetch Cosette."

Cosette, meanwhile, had run to her shoe on waking and found the gold piece, a new twenty-franc coin of the Restoration. She did not know what it was and hid it as if stolen, but she guessed where it came from; the doll and the coin frighten her, only the stranger reassures her, and for the first time in the five years she can remember she feels that she is not alone. Madame Thénardier fetches her from the stairs without a blow or an insult. The stranger unties his bundle: a little woollen gown, apron, bodice, kerchief, petticoat, stockings and shoes, a complete outfit for a girl of seven, all black, and tells her to dress quickly. As day breaks, Montfermeil sees a poorly dressed old man leading a little girl in mourning with a pink doll in her arms along the road toward Livry. Many do not recognize Cosette out of her rags. She does not know with whom she is going or where, only that she is leaving the Thénardier tavern; no one says goodbye. She walks gravely, looking at the sky and now and then at the louis in her new apron pocket, and feels as if she were beside the good God.

title: He Who Seeks to Better Himself May Render His Situation Worse
summary: Stung by his wife's "Is that all?", Thénardier runs after the pair with the fifteen hundred francs, meaning to extort more, and catches them resting in the forest. The stranger answers his demand for a written authorization by producing a note signed by Fantine ordering Cosette to be handed to the bearer, and reckons to the sou that Thénardier has already been overpaid. When Thénardier demands a thousand crowns, the man takes Cosette's hand and his cudgel and walks into the woods; Thénardier follows at a distance until a look sends him home.
details: A quarter of an hour after the departure Thénardier shows his wife the three notes, and for the first time in their marriage she criticizes him: "Is that all?" He agrees he is a fool, calls for his hat and runs out, first in the wrong direction. The man, he reasons, is "a million dressed in yellow" who gave twenty sous, then five francs, then fifty, then fifteen hundred with equal readiness and would have given fifteen thousand; and the mourning clothes ready in the bundle mean a mystery, and the secrets of the rich are sponges of gold to be squeezed. Told they went toward Gagny, he strikes through the forest, stops to curse himself for not bringing his gun, and goes on anyway. Hugo pauses on Thénardier as a double nature: in calm times the makings of a respectable tradesman, and given the right shock, every requisite of a blackguard, a shopkeeper with a taint of the monster.

Beyond the ponds, on the turf path above the old aqueduct of the Abbey of Chelles, he spots the man's hat over the brushwood and the head of the doll beside it; the stranger is letting Cosette rest. Thénardier walks round and presents himself, breathless and respectful, with the fifteen hundred francs: he is taking Cosette back. Cosette shudders and presses against the old man, who repeats slowly, "You are going to take back Co-sette?" Thénardier explains that he is an honest man, that the child belongs to her mother and he can give her up only to the mother, or, if the mother is dead, to someone bringing a paper signed by her naming the person to receive the child. The man reaches into his pocket; Thénardier shivers with joy, expecting a bribe. Instead the man takes out a single small paper and hands it to him: "You are right; read!" It is a note dated Montreuil-sur-Mer, 25 March 1823, addressed to Monsieur Thénardier, instructing him to deliver Cosette to the bearer and promising payment for all the little things, signed Fantine. Thénardier recognizes the signature, and is told he may keep the paper as his receipt. He mutters that the signature is fairly well imitated, and lets it go.

He tries a last effort: he must be paid for all those little things, a great deal is owing. The man rises, dusting his sleeve, and recites the account: in January the mother owed a hundred and twenty francs; in February Thénardier sent a bill for five hundred and received three hundred at the end of February and three hundred at the start of March; nine months since at the agreed fifteen francs a month make a hundred and thirty-five; so he had already been paid a hundred too much, thirty-five remained owing, and he has just received fifteen hundred. Thénardier feels the steel jaw of the trap, shakes himself like a wolf, drops all ceremony, and announces that he will take Cosette back unless he is given a thousand crowns. The stranger says tranquilly, "Come, Cosette," takes her by the left hand and picks up his cudgel with the right. Thénardier notes the size of the cudgel and the solitude of the spot, and stands speechless as they walk into the forest; looking from the man's huge shoulders and fists to his own thin arms, he again regrets the gun, "since I was going hunting."

He does not quite give up: he follows at a distance to learn where they are going, left with an irony, the paper signed Fantine, and a consolation, the fifteen hundred francs. The man leads Cosette toward Livry and Bondy, slowly, head bowed, turning now and then to look back, and when he sees Thénardier he plunges with the child into the brushwood. Thénardier closes in, but at the thickest point the man wheels round and looks at him uneasily, then goes on; two or three hundred paces later he turns again with so sombre a look that Thénardier judges it useless to go further and retraces his steps.

title: Number 9,430 Reappears, and Cosette Wins It in the Lottery
summary: Jean Valjean was not dead: unchained, he swam from the Orion to a moored boat, hid till night, reached the shore, bought clothes, and made his way by a mole's track through southern France to Paris, where a newspaper told him he was believed drowned. He bought mourning clothes for a little girl, took a lodging, and went to Montfermeil. The evening after rescuing Cosette he brings her into Paris and carries her, asleep with Catherine, toward the Boulevard de l'Hôpital.
details: Jean Valjean was not dead. When he fell, or rather threw himself, into the sea at Toulon he was not ironed; he swam underwater to an anchored vessel with a boat moored to it, hid in the boat until night, swam again to the shore near Cape Brun, and, having money, bought clothes at a country house near Balaguier that specialized in outfitting escaped convicts. Then came an obscure, undulating flight: Pradeaux near Beausset, Grand-Villard near Briançon in the Hautes-Alpes, traces later found in the Ain, in the Pyrenees at Accons, near Périgueux. He reached Paris, and the reader has just seen him at Montfermeil.

His first care in Paris was to buy mourning clothes for a girl of seven or eight and to find a lodging; then he went to Montfermeil, where, the narrator reminds us, he had already made a mysterious trip during his earlier escape, of which the law had caught an inkling. Being thought dead deepened the obscurity around him; when one of the Paris papers reporting his drowning fell into his hands he felt reassured and almost at peace, as if he really had died.

On the evening of the day he took Cosette from the Thénardiers he re-entered Paris at nightfall by the Barrière Monceaux, took a cab to the esplanade of the Observatoire, and from there led her on foot through the dark, deserted streets near the Ourcine and the Glacière toward the Boulevard de l'Hôpital. The day had been strange for Cosette: bread and cheese eaten behind hedges, carriages changed often, stretches on foot. She did not complain, but he felt her dragging more and more on his hand, so he took her on his back; still holding Catherine, she laid her head on his shoulder and fell asleep.
